title: The Pulitzer Prize: A major award!
summary: Josh, Chuck and Ben (co-host Speaker 4) discuss the Pulitzer Prize: its founder Joseph Pulitzer and his endowment to Columbia University, the yellow journalism rivalry with William Randolph Hearst, the award's categories, how entries are submitted and judged by volunteer juries, the board's secrecy and power to override finalists, notable controversies (Janet Cook's Jimmy's World, Alex Haley's Roots, Walter Duranty), and criticism of the awards' subjectivity and bias. Closes with listener mail about a road bump near Haile Selassie's former residence.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open the episode and introduce the Pulitzer Prize as an award with prestige, noting the upcoming ceremony and the pronunciation of the name.

segments.title: Joseph Pulitzer's early life
segments.summary: Background on Joseph Pulitzer: Hungarian-born, Civil War service in the Lincoln Cavalry, becoming a newspaper publisher, buying the St. Louis Dispatch, and taking over the New York World.

segments.title: Pulitzer's poor health and the New York World
segments.summary: Pulitzer's health problems and retreat from editing at a young age while keeping control of the World, which became the first national newspaper.

segments.title: Yellow journalism and the Hearst rivalry
segments.summary: Pulitzer helped create yellow journalism and sensational tabloid-style reporting; his protege William Randolph Hearst competed with him via the New York Journal American, with the Yellow Kid comic rivalry giving the style its name and linked to the Spanish-American War.

segments.title: Founding of the Pulitzer Prizes and Columbia's journalism school
segments.summary: Pulitzer proposed a journalism graduate school to Columbia in 1892, which was later established, and in his 1904 will endowed the prizes with money to Columbia. He died in 1911.

segments.title: Pulitzer's legacy design and original categories
segments.summary: Pulitzer created a board to oversee the prizes and let them evolve, and tied journalism to drama, music, fiction and poetry. The original eight awards were four journalism and four book and drama awards, versus today's twenty-three categories.

segments.title: Pulitzer categories: public service, breaking news, investigative
segments.summary: Overview of the Public Service award (the engraved medal, usually awarded to newsroom organizations), Breaking News Reporting (examples include Denver Post on Columbine and New Orleans Times-Picayune on Katrina), and Investigative Reporting (the Wall Street Journal series on federal regulators' stock conflicts).

segments.title: Pulitzer categories: explanatory, local, national, feature, commentary, criticism
segments.summary: Describes the explanatory, local, national, international and feature writing categories, plus commentary and criticism (Roger Ebert won in 1975, Michiko Kakutani also won).

segments.title: Editorial writing, illustrated reporting, photography and audio
segments.summary: Covers editorial writing, illustrated reporting and commentary (editorial cartoons; Mona Chalabi's Jeff Bezos wealth series), breaking news and feature photography, and the newer audio reporting category.

segments.title: Fiction, history, biography, memoir, poetry and nonfiction categories
segments.summary: Fiction used to be novels and is meant for American life; Andrew Sean Greer's Less is recommended. Discussion of history, biography, memoir/autobiography, poetry and general nonfiction, and that a book must be released in the award year to be eligible.

segments.title: Drama and music categories
segments.summary: Drama winners named include David Mamet and August Wilson. The music prize usually goes to classical recordings, with Kendrick Lamar as the one hip hop winner in 2017; hosts criticize the board's stuffiness.

segments.title: Rock music tangent and entry fees
segments.summary: Light banter about British versus American rock bands, then the hosts joke that their own book did not win because they never submitted it, which costs seventy-five dollars.

segments.title: Eligibility and nomination process
segments.summary: Books must be printed in hard copy to be eligible, self-published ebooks are excluded, and authors can nominate themselves. Journalism must appear in a regularly publishing outlet. Broadcast and documentaries are not yet eligible. Being a finalist is the only other distinction, with about 1,100 journalism and 1,400 book entries per year.

segments.title: Jury process and reading loads
segments.summary: About one hundred volunteer jurors are assigned to twenty-two categories and rotate after a few years. The hosts and Speaker 4 question how jurors read around three hundred fiction books and speculate that each judge reads about thirty.

segments.title: Secrecy and the board's final decision
segments.summary: The judging process is secretive. The Pulitzer board meets in February or March, narrows to three finalists, and can pick a winner outside them or award nothing, as in 2012 fiction (a three-way tie) and the 2021 editorial cartooning prize.

segments.title: Board reassigning entries and George Floyd biography
segments.summary: The board can move entries to other categories with a three-quarters vote; the George Floyd biography was moved to general nonfiction and won there.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Break announcement and a short recurring break bumper.

segments.title: Pulitzer frequent winners and small-paper winners
segments.summary: The New York Times has won 132 Pulitzers, the Washington Post over seventy, and the AP fifty-eight. Smaller papers have won: the Storm Lake Times in 2017 for editorial writing, and the Washington Daily News in 1990 for reporting on tainted drinking water in Washington, North Carolina.

segments.title: Janet Cook and Jimmy's World scandal
segments.summary: Janet Cook's 1981 Washington Post story Jimmy's World about an eight-year-old heroin addict was fabricated; Bob Woodward was assistant managing editor; Cook's resume was checked against her former Toledo Blade employer; she confessed and returned the prize, and Teresa Carpenter then won the 1981 feature writing prize for Death of a Playmate.

segments.title: Roots, Walter Duranty, and other controversies
segments.summary: Alex Haley's Roots won a special citation in 1977 despite unverified family claims and admitted plagiarism; the award was not rescinded. Walter Duranty's 1932 Pulitzer for New York Times Stalin coverage is still criticized and has not been rescinded.

segments.title: Subjectivity, bias and critiques of Pulitzer judging
segments.summary: Discussion of the Politico article The Pulitzer Prize Scam by Jack Schafer, the difficulty of comparing entries in the 2023 editorial writing category, and perceived liberal leanings of winners, with a clarification about Alex Jones.

segments.title: Whether the podcast should enter the Pulitzers
segments.summary: The hosts joke about submitting the podcast or a special series for a Pulitzer.

segments.title: Listener mail: Haile Selassie road bump
segments.summary: A chemistry professor at the College of Wooster writes that a student from Ethiopia told him a road bump near Haile Selassie's former residence is engineered so motorists' heads bow when driving by; the professor did not fully verify it.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank the listener and give the contact address for listener mail; the show credits iHeartRadio.
